text:
[DIN](https://arxiv.org/html/1706.06978) directly precedes candidate-conditioned history pooling: a shared feed-forward activation unit scores each history–target pair, then sums weighted history embeddings. Crucially, weights are **not softmax-normalized**, preserving interest intensity. The pooled vector, candidate and other features feed an MLP click classifier. Its base-model comparison isolates adding local activation; Dice and regularization receive separate comparisons. [DIEN](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.03672) instead extracts history states with a GRU and next-behavior auxiliary loss, computes **softmax-normalized bilinear target–state attention**, and scales a second GRU’s vector update gates through AUGRU. Its final target-conditioned state feeds an MLP. Ablations compare two-layer GRU attention, AIGRU, AGRU, AUGRU, and auxiliary supervision.

[MIR](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.09370) provides a richer reranking precedent: candidate self-attention, bidirectional history encoding, item/feature affinity, personalized temporal decay, and SLAttention with softmax distributions over candidates and history. Concatenated user, candidate, attended-set and attended-history representations feed an MLP. Ablations remove these interactions and decay or replace SLAttention. Computationally, DIN evaluates history–candidate pairs; DIEN additionally runs target-specific recurrent evolution. MIR reports O(CH) set–history interaction cost; ordinary dense candidate self-attention also introduces O(C²) work, suppressing embedding dimensions.

Architectural inference: SASRec’s cached history vector plus dot-product scoring costs O(Cd) after encoding; a dot-attention residual over five recent items adds O(5Cd), excluding learned projections/head. Candidate conditioning itself has strong precedent; the narrower contribution is its bounded-window, zero-initialized residual integration. Controls should match parameters, history window, head and training: uniform pooling; candidate-independent attention; shuffled target queries; softmax versus unnormalized weights; zero versus nonzero initialization; frozen versus jointly trained backbone. Zero initialization preserves baseline scores initially; avoid zeroing every residual layer, which can block learning.
